outcomes: Profile and benchmark PyTorch code with warm-up, synchronization, representative shapes, and separate cold-start measurements.
Distinguish torch.compile JIT optimization from torch.export full-graph capture and rewrite unsupported data-dependent control flow.
Export and verify a model with the current torch.export-based ONNX exporter, including dynamic batch constraints.
Compare quantized and floating-point models by artifact size, latency, memory, and output or task quality.
Build an inference boundary that loads trusted state_dicts, validates inputs, disables autograd, and records model provenance.

sections.title: Profile before choosing an optimization
sections.summary: Operator tables and traces identify where time and memory go; a benchmark determines whether a change improves the actual workload.
body: Begin with a representative eager model and input distribution. Warm libraries and kernels, synchronize accelerators around wall-clock timing, and report a latency distribution rather than one call. Keep preprocessing, host-to-device transfer, model execution, and postprocessing separate unless the end-to-end service boundary intentionally includes all four.

torch.profiler records CPU and accelerator activities and can capture operator shapes, memory, call stacks, and trace events when their corresponding options are enabled. Profiling adds overhead, so use a scheduled window instead of profiling an entire production-like run. Sort by self time to find expensive operators and inspect parent operations before rewriting code.
points: Cold start includes import, weight load, allocation, and possibly compilation.
Warm latency measures repeated execution after initialization.
Accelerator timing requires synchronization or device events.
Peak memory and quality belong beside speed.

code.title: Profile a bounded window
code.source:
import itertools
from torch.profiler import ProfilerActivity, profile, schedule

def profile_inference(run_inference, batches, device):
    # wait + warmup + active requires exactly five or more profiler steps.
    window = list(itertools.islice(batches, 5))
    if len(window) < 5:
        raise ValueError("provide at least five representative batches")

    activities = [ProfilerActivity.CPU]
    if device.type == "cuda":
        activities.append(ProfilerActivity.CUDA)

    with profile(
        activities=activities,
        schedule=schedule(wait=1, warmup=1, active=3, repeat=1),
        record_shapes=True,
        profile_memory=True,
        with_stack=True,
    ) as prof:
        for batch in window:
            run_inference(batch)
            prof.step()

    sort_key = (
        "self_cuda_time_total"
        if device.type == "cuda"
        else "self_cpu_time_total"
    )
    return prof.key_averages().table(sort_by=sort_key)

callouts.title: Profiler time is not benchmark time
callouts.body: Instrumentation changes execution. Use the profiler to choose a target, then measure the optimized path without profiler overhead.

sections.title: Use torch.compile for the same Python runtime
sections.summary: torch.compile captures graph regions at runtime, specializes them with guards, and can fall back to eager Python at graph breaks.
body: Compile a function or module only after eager correctness tests pass. The default inductor backend can fuse operations and generate optimized kernels. The first call pays compilation cost, later calls reuse cached code while guards remain valid, and new shapes or Python values can trigger recompilation.

The conditional notebook is intentionally revealing: a Tensor-dependent Python branch may graph-break or specialize in ways that differ from a full deployment graph. Use fullgraph=True during diagnosis, inspect graph-break and recompile logs, and keep unsupported service orchestration outside the compiled model.

code.title: Check eager parity before timing
code.source:
import torch

def compile_with_parity_check(model, example_input):
    model.eval()
    compiled_model = torch.compile(model)
    with torch.inference_mode():
        expected = model(example_input)
        _ = compiled_model(example_input)  # compile and warm
        actual = compiled_model(example_input)
    torch.testing.assert_close(actual, expected, rtol=1e-4, atol=1e-5)
    return compiled_model

callouts.title: JIT optimization is not an export artifact
callouts.body: torch.compile accelerates execution inside a supported Python/PyTorch environment. It is not the API for producing a portable full graph for another runtime.

sections.title: Use torch.export when deployment needs a full tensor graph
sections.summary: torch.export captures normalized tensor computation ahead of time and records the shape constraints that make the capture sound.
body: Unlike torch.compile, export cannot simply execute an unsupported region through ordinary Python. It must remove Python control flow from the captured program or represent it with an explicit higher-order operator. A branch on x.sum() therefore becomes a useful lesson in rewriting data-dependent logic with torch.cond.

Supply representative example inputs and declare dynamic dimensions instead of assuming one traced batch works for every shape. Run the ExportedProgram module on boundary shapes and compare with eager results. Saved export artifacts are under active development, so pin the producing and consuming PyTorch versions.

sections.title: Package ahead-of-time execution deliberately
sections.summary: AOTInductor can compile an ExportedProgram into a .pt2 artifact, trading runtime compilation for a build-time deployment step.
body: The upstream notebook demonstrates torch.export followed by AOTInductor package creation and loading. This path is valuable when startup latency or non-Python integration matters, but torch._inductor.aoti_compile_and_package and related APIs are documented as beta and can change.

Treat the artifact like a platform-specific build output: record PyTorch version, target device, dynamic-shape contract, compiler options, source checkpoint hash, and verification results. Do not assume an artifact produced for one accelerator or release is portable to another.
points: Export establishes a sound full graph and constraints.
AOT compilation lowers that graph for a target environment.
Loading the artifact still requires input validation and parity tests.
Private-namespace beta calls require exact version pinning.

sections.title: Export ONNX through the current dynamo path
sections.summary: PyTorch 2.13 defaults to the torch.export-based ONNX exporter and can return an ONNXProgram for inspection and saving.
body: Set the model to evaluation mode before export and pass example inputs that match the runtime contract. With dynamo=True, use dynamic_shapes for variable dimensions, leave the output path unspecified to receive an ONNXProgram, and request report or verify options when debugging conversion.

Run eager PyTorch and the target ONNX runtime on several fixed inputs, including dynamic-shape boundaries. Compare names, shapes, dtypes, and numerical outputs. Export success alone does not prove the runtime supports the selected operators, precision, or performance target.

code.title: Create and save an ONNXProgram
code.source:
import torch

def export_single_input_onnx(
    model, example_input, destination="model.onnx", output_name="output"
):
    model.eval()
    batch = torch.export.Dim("batch", min=1, max=64)
    onnx_program = torch.onnx.export(
        model,
        (example_input,),
        dynamo=True,
        dynamic_shapes=({0: batch},),
        input_names=["x"],
        output_names=[output_name],
        verify=True,
    )
    onnx_program.save(destination)
    return onnx_program

callouts.title: Dynamic shapes replaced an older habit
callouts.body: With the dynamo exporter, prefer dynamic_shapes. dynamic_axes belongs to the legacy exporter path.

callouts.title: Verification has optional dependencies
callouts.body: The current exporter needs compatible ONNX and ONNX Script packages, and verify=True executes the result with ONNX Runtime. Pin all three in the lesson environment.

sections.title: Quantize with a quality and hardware hypothesis
sections.summary: Fewer bits can reduce weight memory or accelerate supported kernels, but storage compression and runtime speed are different outcomes.
body: The notebook derives symmetric INT8 quantization by selecting a scale, rounding and clamping integer weights, then dequantizing inside a Linear operation. Keep that derivation because it exposes quantization error. For current production experiments, PyTorch's torchao library centralizes modern quantized tensor and quantize_ workflows.

Choose weight-only, dynamic activation, static, or training quantization from a target-device requirement. Measure serialized artifact size, peak memory, warm latency, and output or task-quality change. A smaller checkpoint can run slower when the backend lacks an efficient kernel or repeatedly dequantizes weights.

code.title: A current torchao weight-only experiment
code.source:
import copy
import torch
from torchao.quantization import Int8WeightOnlyConfig, quantize_

def quantize_and_compare(model, example_input):
    float_model = copy.deepcopy(model).eval()
    quantized_model = copy.deepcopy(float_model)
    quantize_(quantized_model, Int8WeightOnlyConfig())
    with torch.inference_mode():
        reference = float_model(example_input)
        quantized = quantized_model(example_input)
    error = (reference - quantized).abs().max().item()
    return quantized_model, error

callouts.title: Namespace migration matters
callouts.body: The notebook's torch.quantization call is useful historical context. torchao is a separate package, so new experiments must install and pin a release compatible with the selected PyTorch build.

sections.title: Build one safe inference boundary, then choose a runtime
sections.summary: FastAPI, Gradio, C++, ONNX, and ExecuTorch are delivery choices around the same validated model contract.
body: At process startup, reconstruct the architecture, load a trusted state_dict with weights_only=True, move it to the selected device, call eval, and run a fixed smoke input. At request time, validate size and dtype, apply the exact training preprocessing, use inference_mode, bound batch or queue size, and return model and preprocessing provenance with structured errors.

Gradio is useful for an interactive demonstration and FastAPI for a service interface, but both are third-party web layers rather than PyTorch deployment formats. ONNX targets compatible external runtimes; AOT/C++ targets compiled server or desktop execution; ExecuTorch lowers export-compatible programs to .pte files for edge backends. Select from latency, platform, operator support, startup, update, and security requirements.
